messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Police Officer
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Emotional Stress: Situations that make me feel strong emotions, Counterfactual Thinking: I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
  Memory: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Nia is a 35-year-old African American police officer who had been proud of the steadiness she brought to patrol work before she was sexually assaulted by a fellow officer after a late shift. She does not tell the story in a smooth sequence. What comes first is the fluorescent light in the locker room hallway, the smell of sweat and disinfectant, his hand pinning her wrist, and the sharp pain in her hips and shoulders. Other parts disappear when she reaches for them. She knows there are stretches she cannot account for no matter how hard she tries, and those blank spaces trouble her almost as much as what she does remember. When the memories break through, they do not feel distant. Her body hurts in the same places again, and along with the pain comes a surge of rage so strong that she has to grip the edge of a table or leave the room.

In the weeks after the assault, Nia had come to believe that what happened said something unforgivable about her. She compared herself harshly to an imagined stronger, smarter woman who would have seen danger sooner, fought harder, or never ended up alone with him in the first place. The broken, incomplete quality of the memory seemed to confirm this view in her mind: if she could not even hold onto the whole event, maybe she had failed in some essential way. She also felt altered in a way she could not reverse. She described herself as permanently changed for the worse, less sure of her instincts, less solid inside. At the same time, she began to feel cut off from the sense of community that had once anchored her, both in the department and in the wider Black community and family networks that had mattered to her; she felt as if she no longer stood where she used to stand with other people.

Those beliefs began to shape how she moved through her days. Because she was certain that disagreement could escalate into something she could no longer control, she started avoiding conflict wherever she could, even when the situation plainly called for her usual directness. At work, she would let other officers take the lead in tense exchanges and would go quiet in briefings rather than challenge anything. She also began steering away from anything likely to stir strong feeling. She skipped family gatherings if she thought people might ask why she seemed different, kept conversations with her husband on the surface, and shut down topics that touched on intimacy, anger, or fear. Privately she spent long stretches thinking about how her life would have been if that night had not happened—how she might still feel at home in her body, in her marriage, in uniform. That line of thought did not comfort her, but she returned to it repeatedly.

The memories themselves drove more of this narrowing. On shift, a trip down a station corridor or the slap of a locker door could suddenly pull her back to the hallway outside the locker room. When that happened, pain shot through her body and the rage rose so fast that she feared what might show on her face or voice. To keep from feeling that, she avoided parts of the building when she could, swapped tasks, and found reasons not to be alone in certain areas. She also avoided arguments on and off the job because anger felt too close to the fury that came with remembering. What frightened her most was not only the memory, but the sense that if she let herself feel anything fully, she would lose control.

Over months, the loop tightened. Each time she recoiled from a charged conversation or abandoned a situation before emotion rose, she felt further from the person she had been. Each time a memory arrived with pain and rage, the missing pieces and bodily force of it seemed to prove that the assault had damaged her permanently. The more damaged she felt, the more she withdrew from her husband, from colleagues she once trusted, and from the cultural and communal ties that had once made her feel known. She could still perform the visible parts of police work, but it had become a thinner version of herself doing it.

Nia came to treatment after her husband told her he felt he was living beside her rather than with her, and after she left a briefing abruptly when a flash of memory hit so hard she thought she might be sick. She is seeking help now because she is tired of arranging her life around what she cannot bear to feel. At the same time, she is afraid that talking about the assault will make the pain and rage come back in full force, and that if the memory ever becomes complete, it will only confirm what she already believes—that she has been changed for good.
